chapters.title: Prologue
paragraphs: NURSE. (The Nurse of Medea's Children enters.) If only Argo had never sped between the blue Clashing Rocks towards Kolchis-land, if only the pine had never fallen under an axe in Pelion's valleys, and no oars had filled the hands of those princely heroes sent by Pelias to seek the Golden Fleece! Then my mistress Medea would never have sailed to the towers of Iolkos, her entire being trembling with love for Jason. She would never have persuaded the daughters of Pelias to kill their father. Nor would she now be living here in Corinth with her husband and children, delighting the people who welcomed her into exile, and always working for Jason's good. A household's surest protection is a wife who lives in agreement with her husband. Now everything has become hatred; their love has fallen sick. Jason has betrayed my mistress and their little children, and is marrying into royalty: his bride is the daughter of Kreon, who rules this country. Poor Medea, insulted and rejected as a wife, appeals to their sworn promises and that supreme pledge, the clasping of right hands. She calls the Gods to witness the reward Jason has given her. She lies without eating, surrendering her body to sorrow, wearing herself away in tears through all the weary hours since she learned how her husband had disgraced her. She never raises her eyes or turns her face from the ground. Friends offer advice, but she listens no more than a rock or a wave of the sea. Only sometimes she turns her pale neck and, alone, cries for the father she loved, her country and the home she abandoned to come here with the man who now treats her as worthless. Suffering has taught the poor woman what a blessing it is to have kept one's native land. She hates her little ones; the sight of them gives her no happiness. I am afraid she is planning something terrible. She has a fierce spirit that refuses to accept mistreatment. I know her, and fear she may creep silently through the house to her bed and drive a sharpened blade through her own heart, or kill the king and the man who is marrying his daughter, and bring still greater suffering on herself. She is dangerous: whoever makes an enemy of her will have a long wait before singing a song of victory. But here come her boys, finished with their racing games, knowing nothing of their mother's troubles. Young hearts do not care to dwell on sorrow. (The Children's Guardian enters with the boys).

CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. Old servant, long the property of my mistress' household, why are you standing here alone beside the gates, talking to yourself about your troubles? How can Medea bear to have you leave her?

NURSE. Grey-haired keeper of Jason's boys, loyal servants always feel their masters' misfortunes in their own hearts. My grief has grown so great that I longed to come out here and tell the earth and sky what has happened to my mistress.
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. Has the poor woman still not stopped her weeping?
NURSE. Stopped! Her suffering has barely started; its middle is still far away!
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. Poor fool! If a servant may call a master that. She knows so little of the newest disaster.
NURSE. What disaster, old man? Please do not refuse to tell me.
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. Nothing. I wish I had not let that word escape me.
NURSE. No, I beg you by your beard, do not hide it from a fellow slave. If secrecy is needed, I will keep it.

CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. As I came near the marble seats where the old men gather around the sacred spring of Peirênê, I heard someone talking and pretended not to listen. He said that Kreon, the ruler here, would soon expel these boys from Corinthian territory along with their mother. But I cannot say whether the story I overheard is true. I wish it were false.
NURSE. Will Jason allow his children to be treated like that, even though he and their mother are estranged?
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. His old attachments trail a long way behind his new ones in this race. This household has no friend in him.
NURSE. Then we are lost, if a new burden of misery is piled aboard before our ship has been lightened of the old one.
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. But keep quiet about it. This is no time for your mistress to learn the news; do not repeat what I have said.
NURSE. Listen, little ones, to the sort of father you have! I would curse him—but no, he remains my master. Yet towards those who love him his conduct proves him a scoundrel.

CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. What man is any different? Have you only just discovered that everyone loves himself more than his neighbour, some for good reason, others out of greed? So their father, for the sake of a new bride, has no love for these boys.

NURSE. Go indoors, dear children; that will be best. And you, keep them as far away as possible. Do not let them near their mother in this fury. Just now I saw her glaring at them like a bull, as though she meant to hurt them. I know that anger will not die away until its lightning has struck. May she injure her enemies, never those who love her!
MEDEA (BEHIND THE SCENES). What a wretched woman I am! What misery keeps falling on my head! Ah, my pain! Ah, my pain! If only I could die!

NURSE. There, my darlings, just what I warned you of! Your mother's heart is surging! Her anger is surging too: keep out of her sight and do not come close to her. Quickly, get inside. Beware of her thoughts, a litter of wild beasts, and of her ruthless nature, which in its desperation might not spare you. Go in now, as fast as you can. We can plainly see how this cloud of grieving, rising from beginnings hidden from sight, will flare into still fiercer lightning bolts of rage. What will that proud, uncontrollable spirit dare when the spurs of injury stab it? (The Children leave with their Guardian).

MEDEA (BEHIND THE SCENES). Misery! I have endured, endured vile wrongs that deserve to wake, to wake an enormous outcry of grief! Children cursed from birth, offspring of one hated and abandoned, abandoned, go to your destruction! Perish beside your father, and let our house sink into the darkness of its doom!

NURSE. Ah, what share have the babies in their father's crimes, that your hatred should strike them down? Helpless innocents, how terribly I fear what may become of you! The tempers of royalty are frightening! Accustomed to giving orders, never taught to obey, they neither forgive nor let their quarrels sleep. Better to follow life's level road. If I cannot grow old in greatness, let me at least grow old quietly and in peace. There is no sweeter name than "The Mean"; to experience it is sweeter beyond telling. Excessive prosperity has never helped mankind. From its dangerous height the Gods, when their displeasure comes, strike with all the greater force.

chapters.title: Parodos
paragraphs: CHORUS. (The Chorus of Corinthian Ladies enters.) I have heard the daughter of Kolchis crying, the voice of a woman crushed by misery, and still she has not fallen silent. Tell us what has happened to her, old woman. Her sobbing lament travelled out from her chamber through the porch. I cannot, cannot feel happiness while suffering weighs on this household, this house I have loved so dearly.

NURSE. A home? There is no home any longer; it has disappeared. My master is enslaved to his royal bride, while my mistress wastes away all day in her room. Nothing her friends can say lets a single cooling drop of comfort fall upon her heart.

MEDEA (BEHIND THE SCENES). If only the fire of heaven's lightning would come down, come down, and burn straight through my head! What benefit is there now in staying alive? Alas, alas! If only I could finish, finish this life I hate, and throw its whole weight of suffering behind me!

CHORUS. Zeus, Earth, Light, did you hear that? The breath of this most unhappy bride is heavy with lamentation. Distraught woman, can your longing for a happiness that has vanished really make you wish for death to come closer—death, where everything ends? Do not pray for that! If your husband has turned to worship a new love and has become a stranger, do not tear your soul apart over him. Zeus will see that justice is done for you. Do not wear yourself away with excessive anguish, weeping for your husband!

MEDEA (BEHIND THE SCENES). Lady Justice, majestic Artemis, look, look at this. See the wrongs I suffer, I who bound my husband's soul with everlasting oaths so that he could never escape their curse, never escape your vengeance! May I live to see him and his bride, those two and their home together, broken into ruin, into ruin! Wretches, who dare to insult Medea when she has done them no harm! My father, my city, I left you long ago for my own destruction, destruction and disgrace, when I spilled my brother's blood along the road of my escape!

NURSE. Do you hear her words, her appeal to Themis and to Zeus, the protector of suppliants who watches over the oaths of mortal people? My mistress will not quickly put her anger aside and settle for some small revenge.

CHORUS. If only she would come outside to where we are waiting, if only she would listen to our voices, perhaps her spirit would learn to turn away from this furious anger and stop burning for revenge! May my love never become treachery; may I never prove false to my friends! Go into the house and bring your mistress out to us. Tell her that everyone here is her friend. Hurry, before some disaster overtakes the masters of this palace. Her grief is swelling like a storm, rushing towards destruction with a force nothing can resist.

NURSE. I will try. My heart has almost given up hope of persuading her, but love will make me attempt it. My queen glares at any servant who dares approach and speak, like a maddened bull or a lioness lying among her cubs. Nothing can tame her. Anyone would be right to call the ancient singers clumsy craftsmen rather than skilled poets. They composed their songs for celebrations, for the arrival of wine at a feast, when the ringing harp adds melody to life's already happy days. But no musician has ever breathed peace into the dreadful fate of human beings, into their heart-breaking anguish, either through music or through a voice joined to the harp. And yet it is these sorrows that bring death and destruction into so many homes. Surely song would do some good if it healed people's grief. Clear voices sounding over an abundant banquet are wasted: the feast itself already casts a spell, hiding our doom from us and enchanting our pain away. (The Nurse leaves).

CHORUS. I have heard the sighs in the cry of the daughter of Kolchis, her piercing anguish as she weeps for the man who trapped her with false promises and betrayed their love. Armed with the wrongs she has suffered, she reproaches Heaven, calling upon Zeus's Queen of Oaths, whose irresistible bonds drew her away and brought her across the starlit waters, where the sea-mist hangs above the Key of Pontus, to Hellas far across the limitless sea.

chapters.title: First Episode
paragraphs: MEDEA. (Medea comes outside.) Women of Corinth, I have left my house so that you will have no reason to find fault with me. I know many people thought arrogant, some because they carry themselves with proud reserve, others because they shrink from strangers. Some who walk quietly through life are accused of laziness. Human eyes cannot judge fairly: before we have learned another person's heart, we hate them on sight, though they have done us no injury. A newcomer must learn the city's ways. But neither do I admire those born here who make their own laws, rude people who treat their neighbours with contempt. As for me, this blow came without warning and broke my heart. I am ruined; life has lost every pleasure, and I want to die, my friends. The man who meant everything to me—you know it well—my husband, has become the worst of men. Of all living creatures with understanding, surely we women are the most miserable. First we must buy ourselves a husband as though competing at an auction, and in doing so purchase a master for our bodies, which is a still deeper evil. And the risk is enormous: will the man we get be bad or good? A woman is disgraced if she changes husbands, and she cannot reject the one she has. Entering unfamiliar habits and customs, she needs a prophet's knowledge of what she has never been taught: what sort of man will share her bed. If we learn that lesson well, and our husband lives beside us without struggling against the yoke, we are fortunate. Otherwise death is the only remedy. When life at home irritates a man, he goes out and relieves his disgust by turning to a friend or someone his own age. We have only one person, one heart to turn to for consolation. Men say that we remain safely at home while they face spears in battle. They are wrong: I would stand behind a shield twice before facing the danger of childbirth once. But your circumstances and mine are different. This city is yours; you have your father's home, the happiness of daily life and the companionship of friends. I am alone, without a city, insulted by the man who carried me off from a foreign shore. I have no mother, brother or relative to give me a safe harbour against disaster. So this is the favour I ask: if I discover a way, some scheme, to avenge these injuries on my husband, his new bride and the father giving her to him, keep it secret. A woman shrinks from danger, and loses courage at the sight of battle and a sword. But wrong her in the rights of marriage, and no spirit will be thirstier for blood.

CHORUS. I will keep silent. Medea, you would be justified in repaying your husband; your grief is no surprise. But here is Kreon, the country's ruler, coming towards us to announce some fresh command. (Kreon enters).

KREON. Medea, with that dark, threatening look and your anger against your husband, I order you to leave this country in exile, taking both sons with you. Do not delay. I am the judge in this matter, and I shall not return home until I have driven you beyond the borders.

MEDEA. Ah, my misery! I am utterly destroyed! My enemies are chasing me under full sail, and there is nowhere to land out of these waves of disaster. Yet, injured as I am, let me ask one thing: Kreon, why are you sending me into exile?

KREON. I am afraid of you; there is no need to disguise it. I fear you will do my daughter some irreparable harm. Several things give me reason for this fear. You are clever, and skilled in many dangerous arts. You are bitter at being deprived of your husband's bed. And people bring me reports of your threats against the father, the bridegroom and the bride. I mean to protect my head before the blow falls. Better to have your hatred now, woman, than show pity once and bitterly regret it when it is too late.

MEDEA. Kreon, gossip has injured me severely many times before; this is nothing new. A sensible father should never educate his sons beyond the ordinary level of wisdom. Their learning becomes a useless burden and wins them only envy and malice from other people. Bring an unfamiliar insight to fools and they will judge you useless rather than intelligent. Gain a reputation greater than those self-proclaimed clever men, and everyone in the city will detest you. That has been my experience too. Some envy my knowledge; others call me idle, meddlesome or unsociable. Yet my wisdom is hardly exceptional. And you are afraid I will disrupt your joy. You need not fear me, Kreon. I am not someone likely to dare an attack upon rulers. What wrong have you done to me? You have chosen a husband for your daughter, as you pleased. My hatred is for my husband. Your own action was surely prudent? No, I bear no resentment towards your prosperity. Let the wedding go ahead, and may you flourish. Only allow me to go on living in your country. Injured though I am, I shall remain silent, overcome by superior strength.

KREON. Your words sound gentle, but the fear remains in my heart that you are planning harm all the while. I trust you even less than I did before. A woman—or a man—who openly rages is easier to guard against than someone who plots in silence. Leave at once, and spare me your appeals. This is settled. No trick will let you stay among us when you are my enemy.
MEDEA. No, I beg you by your knees, and by your daughter, the bride!
KREON. Your appeals are useless. You will never persuade me.
MEDEA. Will you turn me out, with no respect at all for my pleas?
KREON. Yes. I do not love you more than I love my own family.
MEDEA. My country, how intensely I remember you at this moment!
KREON. Yes, Corinth is dear to me too, after my children.
MEDEA. Alas! What a curse love brings upon human beings!
KREON. A blessing or a curse, I suppose, according to one's luck.
MEDEA. Zeus, let the man responsible for this never escape your notice!
KREON. Get away, you raging fool, and stop causing me trouble.
MEDEA. I have troubles enough already; I do not need any more.
KREON. My servants will soon take hold of you and throw you out.
MEDEA. No, no, do not do that, Kreon, I implore you!
KREON. You seem determined to make a scene of this, woman.
MEDEA. I will leave the country. Staying is not the favour I ask.
KREON. Then why resist? Why not free Corinth of your presence?

MEDEA. Allow me just this one day to remain, to make some plans for our exile and find a place of safety for my little ones, since their father takes no care to provide for them. Have pity on them. You too are a father, and it is fitting that you should show kindness to these children. It is not my own banishment that torments me. I am mourning the disaster that has fallen on them.

KREON. Cruelty is the last thing in my nature. Giving way to pity has spoilt many of my plans. Even now, woman, I know I am making a mistake; still, I will grant your request. But take this warning: if the Sun-god's returning torch finds you and your sons anywhere inside this country's borders, you will die. That promise will not be broken. So, if you must stay, remain for one day. That is too short a time for the deeds I fear. (He leaves).

CHORUS. Unhappy woman! I grieve for your misery, for all the distress and suffering that confront you! Where can you turn? What friendly hand will welcome you among strangers? Where will you find a home, a country willing to receive you and free you from these evils? Medea, with God's hand upon your helm, your ship has been steered into waves of despair that will engulf and wreck you!

MEDEA. Things have gone badly on every side; no one can deny it. But in this matter they have not gone badly at all. Do not suppose that yet. The bride and bridegroom still have a bitter struggle ahead, and those who arranged this marriage have no small troubles waiting for them. Do you think I would ever have humbled myself before that man unless I had something to gain or some deception to practise? I would not have spoken to him or touched his hand. But he has been so foolish that, when exile could have prevented every plan of mine, he has granted this day's reprieve. Before it is over I shall have killed three enemies: the father, his daughter and my husband. I have so many ways to bring them death that I cannot decide which to attempt first, my friends. Shall I burn the bridal chamber, or steal quietly through the house to their bed and drive a sharpened knife into their hearts? One obstacle stands in that path: if they catch me crossing the threshold with my murderous purpose, I shall die and give my enemies a reason to laugh. Best to take the direct route that suits my special skill, and destroy them with poison. Yes. But suppose they are dead: what city will receive me? What host will offer a refuge, a safe home, and protect my life from those who seek revenge? There is no one. I shall wait a little. If some stronghold of safety appears, I will accomplish these deaths through secrecy and cunning. But if misfortune forces me out with no hope left, I shall seize the sword myself, even at the cost of my life, and kill them, daring the reckless deed with my own strong hand. By the Queen of Night, whom I honour above all and have chosen as my partner, Hekatê, who lives beside the dark shrine at my hearth, none of them will torment my heart without regretting it. I shall make their wedding bitter and miserable, their marriage promises bitter, and my banishment bitter for them too. Come on, Medea! Use every scrap of your magical knowledge, every plan and trick. Forward to the terrible deed! This is the moment for courage. Look at the wrongs you have suffered. You must not let the sons of Sisyphus or Jason's bride make a laughing-stock of you, a king's daughter, descended from the Sun! You know what means to use. Yes, they say it is women's nature to be helpless in doing good, but wonderfully skilful in devising evil.

CHORUS. The sacred rivers are creeping uphill, back towards their springs. Justice has become injustice, and the old order has dissolved into confusion. Men's hearts think only of betrayal; belief in the Gods reels from its ancient foundations and turns to falsehood. Changes, changes! The people's voice will now bestow honour on me. Glory will shine across my life. The old story about women is over: its age-worn slanders will no longer bind us like chains. Those songs of earlier generations, forever accusing women of treachery and broken faith, will falter in shame. Alas, why have our lips not been touched with the fire of song from the altar of Phœbus, king of the harp and giver of inspiration! Then I would raise my own clear song to challenge men's. Through all the ages there are women to make poets proud, heroines worthy of their verses. But you sailed far across the foam from your ancient home, driven by a heart gone wild. You saw the gates of the sea, the Twin Rocks, open apart. Now in a stranger's country you must wake to an empty marriage bed, abandoned by your husband, overtaken by misery, and driven out in disgrace. Oaths have lost their binding power. Wide Hellas has no shame left for promises betrayed; shame has flown away to heaven. You have no father's house to offer harbour when the storms of trouble gather. Another woman has seized your bridal chamber, and now, in the pride of her power, rules over you, unhappy one.

chapters.title: Second Episode
paragraphs: JASON. (Jason enters.) This is far from the first time I have seen the terrible harm a stubborn temper can cause. You could have stayed here, in this country and this home, if you had quietly accepted your rulers' decisions. Instead, your reckless outbursts have brought you exile. I am not offended: keep shouting, "Jason is the worst of men!" as long as you please. But after what you said against the rulers, consider yourself fortunate that banishment is your only punishment. I kept trying to calm the anger of the royal family; I wanted you to remain. You would not restrain your foolishness, but went on insulting those in power, and that is why you must leave. Still, I have not grown tired of caring for my own people. I have come, woman, out of concern that when you and the children are exiled, you should lack neither money nor anything else. Exile brings plenty of troubles with it. You may hate me, but I could never wish harm upon you.

MEDEA. Scoundrel beyond all scoundrels! That is the darkest name my tongue can find for your cowardice. You come to me—you actually come, after proving yourself hateful to heaven, to me and to the whole human race! To injure those who love you and then look them in the face is neither boldness nor courage. It is shamelessness, the worst disease that infects mankind. Still, I am glad you came. I shall lighten my heart by abusing you, and listening will make you suffer. Let me begin at the beginning. I saved your life. Every Greek who sailed beside you in Argo knows it. You were sent to put the fire-breathing bulls under the yoke and sow a field of death. I killed the dragon that guarded the Golden Fleece, coiling round it without ever sleeping, and brought the light of rescue to you. I abandoned my own father and my home, and followed you to Iolkos beneath Pelion, more devoted to your cause than wise. I killed Pelias by the hands of his own children, the worst of deaths, and so relieved you of every fear. After all I did for you, you vilest man, you deserted me for a new bride, though I had borne your children. If you had been childless, your hunger for another marriage might have been forgivable. But faith in oaths has disappeared. I do not know whether you think the ancient Gods still rule, or whether new laws have been made for men. Your own heart must tell you that you have broken your promises to me. Shame on this right hand you so often clasped, and these knees! How uselessly a worthless man embraced us; how he has cheated our hopes! Come, I will speak with you as a friend, though what fair treatment can I expect from you? Still, I shall question you, and your answers will expose you further. Where can I go now? To my father's house, which I deserted along with my country for your sake? To the unfortunate daughters of Pelias? How warmly they would welcome their father's murderer! That is how things stand: I have made my own family my enemies, and to serve you I have turned against me people I should never have hurt. What happiness you have given me among the women of Hellas in repayment for it all! What a marvellously faithful husband I possess—miserable woman that I am!—if I must leave this country friendless, alone in exile with my lonely children. A splendid disgrace for our new bridegroom: his babies and the woman who saved him wandering in poverty! Zeus, why have you given men clear ways to recognise counterfeit gold, but left no natural stamp on a man's body by which we can identify the worthless?
CHORUS. Anger is a terrible thing, beyond the reach of any healing remedy, when people who once loved one another meet as bitter enemies.

JASON. It seems I must speak skilfully. Like a cautious sailor with his canvas reefed, I must run before the storm of abuse coming from your tongue, woman. You pile your services as high as a tower, but I credit Kypris alone, no other God or human being, with saving my voyage. You are clever; must you force me to explain how Love's arrows, which never miss, compelled you to preserve my life? Still, I will not press that point too closely. You saved me, and that was a good deed. Yet you received more than you gave by rescuing me, as I shall show. First, you now live in Hellas instead of a barbarian country. You understand justice and have learned to live under law rather than force. All the Greeks have heard of your wisdom; you have a famous name. Had you remained at the world's remote edge, no one would be telling your story. I would want neither a house full of gold nor a voice sweeter than Orpheus's if fame never heard about my good fortune. That is enough about my great struggles, since you challenged me to this dispute. As for your attacks on my royal marriage, I shall show, first, that I acted wisely; second, with self-control; and third, as the best friend you and my children could have. No, listen until I finish. When I arrived here from Iolkos, followed by so many desperate misfortunes, what greater stroke of luck could an exile find than marriage to a princess? It was not, as you resentfully imagine, because I hated your bed and desired a new bride. Nor did I want a larger number of children: those I have are enough, and I find no fault in them. I wanted us to live respectably, a matter of real importance, and without hardship. I know very well how friends keep their distance from a poor man. I wanted to raise our sons as befits my family, and give your children brothers, joining them all into one household so that we could live happily. What need have you for more children? But it helps me to use sons yet to be born to support the ones already living. Was that such a bad plan? You would not say so if the loss of your marriage bed did not sting you. You women are so unreasonable: while your marriage rights remain intact you believe everything is well, but if anything goes wrong in bed, you turn bitterly against even the finest, most fortunate circumstances. If only people could have children by some other means, without the existence of women, mankind would never have suffered this curse.
CHORUS. Words, Jason, cleverly dressed-up words. Yet to my mind—and I know you will dislike hearing it—you are behaving unjustly by betraying your wife.

MEDEA. On many subjects my judgement differs from most people's. To me, a villain with a clever tongue loses far more than he gains. Certain that his eloquence can cover his wrongdoing, he becomes bolder in wickedness. That is no great wisdom. So do not try your handsome appearances and cunning speeches on me. One statement will defeat you: if you were not a scoundrel, you would have obtained my agreement to this marriage instead of hiding it from those close to you.
JASON. Yes, you would have been a wonderful help with my plans if I had mentioned marriage, when even now you cannot control this enormous rage!
MEDEA. That was not what stopped you. A foreign wife would bring you no honour as you grew older.

JASON. Understand this clearly: I did not marry the princess I have won out of desire for her. As I told you, I wanted to protect you and father royal children, brothers for my sons and a strong defensive tower for my household.
MEDEA. I want no prosperous life overshadowed by sorrow, no good fortune with the thorns of conscience piercing my heart!
JASON. Can you change your prayer to something wiser? Pray that you never mistake a benefit for a grief, or think yourself unfortunate when good luck comes.
MEDEA. Yes, go on insulting me! You have a place of safety, while I am driven from this country abandoned and alone.
JASON. This was your own choice. Put the blame on no one else.
MEDEA. My choice? By marrying someone else and betraying you, I suppose!
JASON. By uttering wicked curses against the royal family.
MEDEA. Quite so. And in the same way I am cursing your household now?

JASON. I will argue with you about this no further. But if you are willing to accept money from me to help you or the children in exile, say so. I am ready to give generously, and provide tokens of hospitality that will secure you friends. You would be foolish to refuse. Restrain your anger, and you will find yourself better off.
MEDEA. Your friends! I want nothing to do with friends of yours. I will accept nothing, and you must offer nothing. A scoundrel's gifts bring no benefit.

JASON. At any rate, I call the Gods as witnesses that I am willing to give you and your sons every assistance. But you dislike what would help you; your stubborn pride rejects friends. You will suffer all the more for it.

MEDEA. Go away! While you linger at these doors, impatience for your newly captured bride is burning you up! Marry her. Perhaps—and may God make my words come true—you will have a wedding you would gladly undo. (Jason leaves).

CHORUS. Love brings men neither glory nor honour when it arrives in unchecked excess. But when Kypris descends and lets her joy fall in moderation, no Goddess is more enchanting. Queen, do not aim at me from your golden bow that inescapable arrow poisoned with desire—never at me! Let self-restraint protect me, that loveliest gift of the immortal Gods. May Love's Queen never visit me in terror, bringing bitter conflict and unforgiving feuds, striking my soul with frenzied restlessness over a mismatched bed. May she honour the peace of marriage instead, and with her sharp sight choose the best bonds for us. My country, my home, may exile never be my fate! May my feet never be led down the hard roads of poverty! That would be suffering most worthy of pity. Before that, let death, let death end the struggle of living and close life's brief day! There is no sharper agony than being cut off like that from one's homeland. We have seen it ourselves and need no one else to teach us: no city, no friend has shown you compassion in your dreadful affliction. But the man who has no regard for those who love him, who will not unlock his heart honestly for the unfortunate, may he perish cursed and hated. Such a man will never be my friend!

chapters.title: Third Episode
paragraphs: AIGEUS. (Aigeus enters.) Greetings, Medea! No one knows a better word than that for welcoming a friend.
MEDEA. And greetings to you, Aigeus, son of wise Pandion. Where have you come from on your journey through this country?
AIGEUS. I have just left the ancient prophetic shrine of Phœbus.
MEDEA. What took you to that prophetic centre, the navel of the earth?
AIGEUS. I went to ask how I might become the father of children.
MEDEA. By heaven! Have you really remained without children all this time?
AIGEUS. I have none; some God's will has brought me that fortune.
MEDEA. Are you married, or have you never shared a marriage bed?
AIGEUS. No, I too have been yoked to the bed of marriage.
MEDEA. And what did Phœbus tell you about having descendants?
AIGEUS. Profound, wise words that no human being can explain.
MEDEA. Could I hear the God's answer without committing a sin?
AIGEUS. Certainly. Indeed, it needs a wise mind more than anything.
MEDEA. What were his words? Tell me, if hearing them is permitted.
AIGEUS. He said I must not loosen the projecting foot of the wine-skin.
MEDEA. Until you had done what, or arrived in which country?
AIGEUS. Until I had returned to the hearth of my ancestors.
MEDEA. Then what purpose brought you sailing to this coast?
AIGEUS. There is a man named Pittheus, the king of Trœzen.
MEDEA. Pelops' son, reputed to be a man of great religious devotion.
AIGEUS. I want to repeat the God's answer to him.
MEDEA. Yes, he is wise and understands matters of this kind.
AIGEUS. And he is the dearest of my allies in war.
MEDEA. Then may you prosper and obtain what your heart longs for.
AIGEUS. Why are your eyes lowered? Why do you look so pale and worn?
MEDEA. Aigeus, my husband is the most contemptible of all men.
AIGEUS. What do you mean? Explain plainly what is hurting you.
MEDEA. Jason is wronging me, though I have done him no wrong.
AIGEUS. What has he done to you? Tell me more clearly.
MEDEA. He is marrying another woman to make her mistress of his home.
AIGEUS. What! Has he actually dared to do something so shameful?
MEDEA. Yes. He once loved me; now he treats me with contempt.
AIGEUS. Has he fallen in love again, or come to hate you?
MEDEA. In love? Yes, with the highest things: he has betrayed love itself!
AIGEUS. Then let him go to ruin if he is so worthless!
MEDEA. What he fell in love with was a connection to royalty.
AIGEUS. Who is giving him a daughter? Finish telling me the story.
MEDEA. Kreon, the man who rules this country of Corinth.
AIGEUS. Lady, you certainly have good reason for your sorrow.
MEDEA. It is killing me! And on top of that I am being banished.
AIGEUS. By whom? This is another misfortune you are telling me about.
MEDEA. Kreon is driving me out of Corinth into exile.
AIGEUS. Does Jason let him do it? I cannot approve of that.

MEDEA. He pretends to object, but as for standing firm—never! Now I beg you, taking hold of your beard and clasping your knees as your suppliant: have pity, pity on my unhappy fate. Do not stand by while I am driven out without a home. Give me a place at the hearth in your land and in your house. May heaven then bless your marriage with children, and bless you also at your death. You do not know what good fortune you have encountered. I will put an end to your childlessness and make your seed grow into sons: I know medicines that can do this.

AIGEUS. There are many reasons, lady, why I am inclined to grant this favour. First, respect for the Gods; then, the children you promise, for in that respect the name of Aigeus is entirely extinguished. Here is my offer: if you come to my country, I will undertake your defence within the bounds of justice. But I must warn you of this. I will not agree to take you away from this land myself. If you reach my home by your own efforts, you will remain in safety, and I will hand you over to no one. You must make your own escape from here, because I also wish to remain blameless towards my allies.
MEDEA. I accept. But if you would pledge this to me with an oath, I would have everything I ask of you.
AIGEUS. What, do you not believe me? Or what difficulty still troubles you?

MEDEA. I do believe you. But Kreon and the family of Pelias are my enemies. Bound by an oath, you could never surrender me to them when they tried to drag me out of your country. If you only promised, without making a pledge to the Gods, you might become their friend and readily obey a herald's demand. My cause has no strength. They have wealth and a royal household on their side.

AIGEUS. Your words show extraordinary foresight, lady! Still, if you wish it, I will not refuse. It is safer for me too, giving me a reason I can present to your enemies, while making your position more secure. Name the Gods by whom I should swear.
MEDEA. Swear by the wide Earth, and by the Sun, my father's father, and include the entire company of Gods.
AIGEUS. What am I promising to do, or to refrain from doing? Tell me.
MEDEA. That you will never expel me from your country yourself, and if any enemy tries to drag me away, you will never, while you live, consent to surrender me.
AIGEUS. I swear by Earth, by the Sun in his pure majesty, and by every God, to keep the promise you have described.
MEDEA. That is enough. What punishment if you break your pledge?
AIGEUS. Whatever punishment falls on men who hold the Gods in contempt.
MEDEA. Continue happily on your journey; everything is settled. I too will come to your city as quickly as I can, once I have accomplished my purpose and obtained my desire. (Aigeus leaves).

CHORUS. May Maia's son, the ruler of travellers, bring you safely home. Aigeus, may the dream in your heart, the sweet visions that give wings to your feet, come to fulfilment. What you have done today has shown me the nobility of your nature.

MEDEA. Zeus, Justice born of Zeus, and radiance of the Sun, now, my friends, we shall overcome our enemies. We have set our feet upon the road. Now there is hope of taking revenge. Where my plans were weakest, this man has appeared as a harbour in the storm. I shall fasten my ship's stern-rope to him when I reach the city and stronghold of Pallas. Now I will tell you my entire plan, though I do not expect it to please you. I shall send someone from my household to ask Jason to come and see me. When he arrives, I shall speak gently, saying, "I want what you want," and, "This is a good thing." I shall say his royal marriage, his betrayal of me, benefits us and was very wisely arranged. I shall ask for my sons to be allowed to stay. Not because I would leave my children in an enemy country to be trampled on, but because I mean to use this deception to kill the king's daughter. I shall send them to the bride with gifts in their hands, a finely woven robe and a golden crown, to win exemption from banishment. If she accepts my ornaments and puts them on, she will die horribly, and so will anyone who touches her. Such terrible poisons will coat my gifts. But I pass over that part now and mourn the deed I still must carry out. I shall kill my children—yes, my own. No one will tear them from my hands. Then, when I have destroyed Jason's entire household, I shall leave this country, fleeing the blood of my dear little ones, having dared an utterly unholy act. I cannot endure the laughter of my enemies. Let everything go. What does life mean to me? I have no country, no home, no shelter from my troubles. My mistake was made that day when, deceived by this Greek's words, I abandoned my father's house. With God's help, he will pay me back. Never again will he look upon the sons I bore him alive, and he will father no son by his new bride. The wretched woman is doomed to a wretched death from my poisons. Let no one think me powerless, feeble or submissive! I am the opposite: fierce towards my enemies, kind towards those who love me. Such people live the most glorious lives.
CHORUS. Now that you have shared your plan with me, I speak both as someone who wants to help you and as a defender of human laws: do not do this.
MEDEA. It must be done. Still, it is natural for you to say that; you have not been injured as I have.
CHORUS. Woman, will you truly find the heart to kill your own sons?
MEDEA. Yes. That is how I can hurt my husband most deeply.
CHORUS. But you would become the most miserable wife of all.

MEDEA. Let it be so. Every word meant to stop me is wasted. You there! (To the Nurse.) Go and bring Jason to me, you whom I trust with every confidential errand. See that you tell no one anything of my intentions, if you are a loyal servant and a woman. (Medea and the Nurse leave).

CHORUS. How fortunate the ancient race of Erechtheus, descendants of the blessed Gods, living in a land untouched by devastation and sheltered in peace. They drink continually from Wisdom's splendid wine, moving lightly through the shining clear air as if carried on wings. There, the story says, golden-haired Harmonia gave birth to the nine stainless Pierid Muses. And they tell how the Lady of Cyprus drew from the beautifully flowing Cephisus and breathed the waters' dew far across the land on the sweet winds of Zephyr. She sends her Loves, seated in glory beside Wisdom, to shape the whole story of virtue, while over her hair she throws, throws fresh garlands of fragrant roses. (Medea returns.) How could that holy city, the city of sacred waters, which stretches out a protecting hand to every friend travelling through its country, receive an accursed murderess who pitilessly slaughtered her babies, a pollution among its daughters? Set the thought before your mind: to murder the children of your own womb! Think what it means to kill your sons, what a deed you would commit today! We beg you by your knees, we implore you by earth and heaven: do not bring such a fate upon your little ones! Where, where will you find the desperate hardness to serve so fiendish a purpose, to stiffen your heart and steady your hand so that it does not turn aside from the merciless act that will stain you with the horror of children's blood? When you turn your eyes upon your little ones, how will you restrain the mother within you and stop the tears from rising? Can you harden your breast when your children kneel before you, and redden your hand without your heart yearning for the darlings you have killed?

chapters.title: Fourth Episode
paragraphs: JASON. (Jason enters.) I have come because you sent for me. Though you are my enemy, I will not refuse you this favour. I will listen, woman, to whatever fresh request you wish to make.

MEDEA. Jason, forgive what I said before, and bear with that temper of mine. The memory of our former love should make that possible. I have called myself to account and reproached myself: "Miserable woman, why am I behaving like a mad creature? Why am I raging against good advice, quarrelling with the rulers of this country and with my husband, who is acting for my real benefit by marrying into royalty and giving my sons brothers? Why do I not put an end to my anger? What is wrong with me, when the Gods are offering blessings? Have I no children? Do I not know that we are exiles from our own country and have no friends?" Thinking it over, I realised I had been feeding enormous foolishness and anger without reason. Now I approve of you. You seem wise to have secured this family connection for us, while I was senseless. I should have supported your plans, helped with everything, decorated the marriage bed and gladly waited upon the bride. But we are women; there is no need for a harsher name. You should not repay wrong with wrong, or set your own foolishness against mine. I give way and admit I was unwise then, but have now come to a better judgement. Children, my children, leave the house and come here. (The Children enter.) Come and greet your father; join me in saying goodbye to him. With your mother, put the old hatred aside and make peace with those who love you. We have called a truce; bitterness has given way. Take his right hand. Oh, the evils lying in ambush! The shadow of things hidden keeps haunting me! My children, will you live for many years and still stretch loving arms towards him like this? Ah, how quickly my tears come, how frightened I am! The quarrel with your father is over—so late, so late!—and my softening eyes have filled with tears.
CHORUS. Tears of frightened sorrow are springing into my eyes as well. May nothing worse than what has happened yet befall us!

JASON. Woman, I welcome this mood, though I do not condemn the earlier one. It is natural for women to grow angry when their husband negotiates another marriage. But your heart has turned towards better thoughts now, and though late, you have cast your vote for the winning side. That is a wise woman's action. As for you, children, your father has taken considerable thought for you, carefully, and may heaven help him. I believe you and your brothers will one day stand foremost in this land of Corinth. Grow strong; your father, with whatever God favours us, will arrange the rest. May I see you grown tall and handsome, in the prime of manhood, victorious over my enemies. But why are you wetting your eyes with sorrowful tears, turning your pale face away from the children? Why do you not welcome what I say with happiness?
MEDEA. It is nothing. My heart is simply dwelling on these children.
JASON. Do not be afraid. I will make every arrangement for their good.
MEDEA. I will try. It is not that I doubt your promises. But a woman is only a woman, born to weep.
JASON. Poor woman, why are you making these laments over them?

MEDEA. I gave birth to them. When you prayed for their lives, pity came over me, whispering, "Will it happen?" But I have told you only part of what I asked you here to discuss. Let me say the rest. Since the king wishes to expel me from this country, I know perfectly well that leaving is best for me too. I should not remain as an obstacle to you and the rulers, whose household regards me as an enemy. So I will go into exile. But plead with Kreon not to banish my sons, so that you can raise them yourself.
JASON. I may not succeed in persuading him, but I must make the attempt.
MEDEA. Then ask your bride to appeal to her father, so that your sons are not driven out of this land.
JASON. Certainly. And I think I can persuade her, if she has anything in common with other women.

MEDEA. I will help you in that effort. I shall send her gifts whose beauty, I know, far surpasses anything people see today: a finely woven robe and a golden crown. Our sons will carry them. An attendant must bring the ornaments here immediately. Her blessings will be countless, not merely one: she gains you as her husband, a matchless spouse, and possesses ornaments the Sun, my father's father, once gave to his own descendants! Take these wedding presents in your hands, my sons. Carry them to the fortunate princess-bride and give them to her. These gifts will surely satisfy her.

JASON. But, foolish woman, why strip yourself of these treasures? Do you think a royal household lacks robes, or gold? Keep them; do not give them away. If my wife values me at all, I am certain she will prefer my request to any treasures.

MEDEA. Do not say that. Gifts persuade even the Gods, so people say. Gold weighs more with human beings than endless words. Fortune is hers; God favours her cause now, and her power is newly born. I would pay with my life to buy my sons' release from exile, not merely with gold. Now, children, go into that wealthy house. Appeal to your father's new wife, my lady and queen. Ask not to be exiled, and give her my ornaments. The most important thing is that she should take the gifts into her own hands. Hurry, and return to your mother with happy news that she has obtained what she longs for. (Jason and the Children leave).

CHORUS. My hope for the children's lives has changed into despair. There is no hope left! Already they are walking the road to slaughter! The bride will accept that garland of a crown, its glittering beauty concealing destruction for the unhappy woman. She will take it between her hands to place an ornament of Hades upon her golden hair. Its dazzling loveliness, its unearthly splendour, will quickly tempt her to dress herself in the robe and the crown worked in gold. Soon she will stand arrayed as a bride before phantoms risen from Hades. Such a terrible trap will catch her feet. The poor woman will be swallowed by her appointed death, and never again steal out of Doom's dark prison. And you, wretched bridegroom, cursed in your eagerness for a royal alliance, you are bringing destruction on your sons' lives without knowing, without thinking! Your bride will pledge herself to a hideous death. How far you are sinking from your old good fortune! Amid my laments I grieve too for your anguish, unhappy mother, preparing to slaughter your own little ones in revenge upon the man who would marry another unlawfully and abandon you to live beside a king's daughter. (The Children's Guardian returns with the Children).
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. Mistress, your sons are freed from the sentence of exile! The royal bride gladly took your present into her hands. Your sons have peace now.
MEDEA. What misery!
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. Why are you standing there stunned when things have gone well? Why turn your face away, instead of listening happily to the news I bring?
MEDEA. How wretched I am!
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. That cry does not fit the news I have brought you.
MEDEA. Misery, and misery again!
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. Have I unknowingly brought bad news? Was I mistaken in thinking this a happy message?
MEDEA. Your news is what it is. I do not blame you for it.
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. Why are your eyes cast down? Why are you shedding tears?
MEDEA. They must fall, old man. The Gods and I together—fool that I am!—have arranged these matters badly.
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. Take courage. Your children may still bring you back to your home.
MEDEA. Before that happens, I in my misery shall send others home.
CHILDREN'S GUARDIAN. You are not the only mother parted from her sons. Human beings must bear misfortune with submission.

MEDEA. I will. But go inside and prepare what the children need for their daily life. (The Children's Guardian leaves.) Children, children, you have a city and a home where you will live, leaving your wretched mother behind, deprived of her forever. I must go into exile in another country before I have enjoyed you and seen your happiness, before I have prepared your marriage beds, dressed your brides and bridal rooms, and lifted the wedding torch. What a curse this merciless temper has brought upon me! For nothing, for nothing, my babies, I raised you. All for nothing I wore myself out in labour and endured the sharp pains of giving you birth. Ah, the hopes I had, unhappy woman! I hoped your hands would care for me in old age, that I would die enclosed in your loving arms, as everyone desires! But that sweet dream is over, over! Deprived of you, I shall waste away a bitter, sorrowful life. You will pass into another life and never again look lovingly upon your mother. Woe! Woe! Why are your eyes fixed on me, my darlings? Why are you smiling at me for the very last time? Alas! What am I to do? My heart gives way when I look at my children's laughing eyes! Women, I cannot do it! Goodbye to those plans! I shall take my children out of this land. Why should I wound their father's heart through their suffering, only to bring twice as much suffering on myself? I will not, I will not! Farewell, my plans! But—but what is happening to me? Am I willing to be laughed at, to let my enemies slip from my hands without punishment? I must dare to act. Shame on the cowardice that let these tender words escape my heart! Children, go indoors. (The Children leave.) Anyone who cannot witness my sacrifice without sin must answer for himself. My hand will not tremble. Oh! Oh! My heart, my heart, do not do this deed! Let them live, miserable heart; spare your babies! Living there with me, they will bring you joy. No! By the demons below who dwell with Hades, I will never leave my children for my enemies to trample upon. They have to die. And since it has to happen, I who gave them life will kill them. All of this is fixed destruction: she will not escape! Even now the crown is on her head, and the royal bride is dying in my robe. I know it. But since I must set out on a most unhappy journey, and send these children on one still more unhappy, I want to speak to my sons. (The Children return.) Give me your right hands, my babies; let your mother kiss them. Hands I love so dearly, lips so dear to me, my children's bodies and noble faces, may blessings be yours there! Your father has robbed you of everything here. Sweet, sweet embrace! Your rose-petal skin, your fragrant breath! Go away, go away! I have no strength left to look at you; evil has overwhelmed me. (The Children leave.) Now, now I understand the horrors I intend. But passion masters clear judgement, and this is what brings the most dreadful evils upon humanity.

CHORUS. Often before now my mind has climbed lonely heights of thought, the steep paths of heaven, or plunged deep into darkness where a woman's weaker heart has failed. But why should it fail? Should no inspiration stir a woman's breast? Should she never welcome that sweet visitor, Song, which gives voice to Wisdom's thought? Alas! Not every woman can! Few, very few—perhaps you might find one in a thousand—have an inward daylight kindled by poetry's sun. Now I say this: quiet happiness that has never known love's fever in the blood, or the pains and joys of motherhood, surpasses the joy mingled with worry that parents know. Those without children never discover whether babies bring sunshine or cloud to human lives; the labour and grief of parental love lie far beyond their knowledge. But those whose houses ring with children's sweet laughter I see constantly fretted by anxiety, always working to provide a fitting upbringing for those they love. A person labours with love stronger than death. Yet, yet, who can know whether the heir to whom all that wealth will pass will be wise or foolish? Last comes the worst thing of all. Even if you acquire enough wealth, even if your sons grow into fine, good men, what if cruel Death carries their lives down and disappears into Hades? What benefit is there in Heaven laying this upon mankind, on top of everything else, this crowning sorrow?

chapters.title: Exodos
paragraphs: MEDEA. Friends, I have waited a long time to learn what fortune will bring from that place. Look, I see one of Jason's servants coming towards us. My expectant heart tells me he is bringing news of fresh disaster. (A Messenger enters).
MESSENGER. Medea, you who have committed a dreadful, unlawful act, escape, escape. Once you have boarded a ship or a chariot that races over the plain, do not leave it for a moment.
MEDEA. What has happened to make such an escape necessary?
MESSENGER. The princess has just died, and her father Kreon is dead as well, both killed by your poisons.
MEDEA. What splendid news you bring. From this moment I count you among my friends and benefactors.
MESSENGER. What are you saying? Are you sane, or have you lost your mind? You hear that the royal household has been destroyed and feel pleasure, with no fear at all?
MEDEA. Yes, I could answer you with an argument of my own. But do not hurry away, my friend. Tell me how they died. You will make me twice as happy if their deaths were especially horrible.

MESSENGER. When your two children arrived with their father and entered the rooms decorated for the wedding, those of us servants who grieved for your troubles were pleased. News of a truce in the old quarrel between you and your husband immediately began to whisper from ear to ear. One person kissed your sons' hands, another their golden heads. Happiness drew me after them into the women's rooms. The woman we now honoured in your place, before she saw your pair of sons yoked together like a chariot team, kept turning longing eyes towards Jason. Then she drew her veil across her face and twisted her pale neck away contemptuously, disgusted by the approach of your children. Your husband tried to soften the girl's anger and hostility. He said, "Do not treat your friends as enemies. Stop being angry and turn your head back. Regard as friends the people your husband regards as friends. Accept their presents, and ask your father to cancel their exile, for my sake." When she saw the finery, she could not resist and agreed to everything her husband asked. Before the father and your boys had gone far from her room, she took the richly worked clothes and dressed herself, setting the golden crown around her curls. She arranged her hair before a bright mirror, smiling at the phantom image of herself. Then she rose and walked through the rooms, taking dainty steps on ivory feet, delighted with her gifts and repeatedly glancing down from her neck to the hem at her ankles. What followed was terrible to see. Her colour changed suddenly. She staggered backwards, her limbs trembling, and barely managed to drop onto a couch before she fell to the floor. An old serving-woman, thinking perhaps that Pan or another God had sent this seizure, raised a cry of prayer. That was before she noticed the white foam bubbling from the girl's mouth, her rolling eyes and her bloodless face. Then the servant gave a different cry, a long, loud scream. At once one person rushed to her father's rooms, another to her new husband, to tell them the bride had been stricken. The whole house echoed with hurrying feet. By then a fast runner straining every limb could have reached the finish of a six-plethra course. She woke from that speechless trance, her eyes having been shut, and gave a shrill, horrible scream, poor woman! Her agony attacked like two armies charging at once. The golden band round her head began shooting out an astonishing stream of ravenous flame, while the delicate clothes your children had given her devoured her pale flesh. She leapt from the couch and ran, all on fire, shaking her head and hair from side to side to throw off the crown. But the gold clasp gripped her firmly. Whenever she shook her locks, the fire blazed with twice the fury. At last, overcome by suffering, she fell to the floor, so disfigured that only a father could have recognised her. The regal calm of her eyes and her lovely features had disappeared. Blood dripped from the top of her head, mingled with sparks of fire. The flesh melted off her bones like resin dripping from a pine, consumed by that mysterious poison. A dreadful sight! Everyone was afraid to touch the body, warned by her hideous fate. Her miserable father, still knowing nothing of what had happened, suddenly entered and threw himself upon her corpse. He began to wail, wrapped his arms around her body, kissed her and cried, "My unhappy child, what God has destroyed you so horribly? Who has robbed this old man, already a tomb, of you? Ah, if only I could die beside you!" When his tears and groans subsided, he tried to raise his aged body, but he clung to those fine robes as ivy clings around laurel branches. Then came a ghastly struggle. As he tried to lift his knee, her body pulled against him. If he dragged himself away by force, he tore his old flesh from his bones. At last he gave up and breathed his last, the unfortunate man unable to resist his destruction any longer. The bodies lie there, the daughter held in her old father's embrace. Tears must mourn that suffering; words cannot. I shall say nothing about your part in it. You will find your own way to escape punishment. But now, as often before, I consider human life a shadow. I am not afraid to say that those who seem wise among us, those skilled in clever speech, are guilty of the deepest foolishness. No mortal is happy. At the high tide of fortune a man may be more prosperous than his neighbour. But happy? No! (He leaves).

CHORUS. I think the God will surround Jason with many disasters today, and justly so. But how pitiful your fate, daughter of Kreon: you have gone down into the halls of Hades because Jason wanted you for his wife!

MEDEA. Friends, I have decided. I shall kill my children quickly and leave this country, instead of delaying and surrendering my sons to death at hands still more merciless. They must die; and since that cannot be avoided, I who gave them life shall also give them death. Come, my heart, prepare yourself for the fight! Why hesitate over the dreadful evil deeds that must be done? My miserable hand, take up the sword. Take it, and move towards this bitter starting-line of life. Do not become cowardly. Do not think of your little ones, of how dearly you love them, or how you gave them birth. Forget your sons for this one short day, then mourn them afterwards. Even if you kill them, they remain beloved, and I remain a wretched woman. (Medea leaves).

CHORUS. Earth, and the Sun's radiance that reveals everything, look down upon an accursed woman before this mother satisfies her thirst for murder, striking with her own hands the tender fruit of her womb. Look down: she comes from your golden lineage, and the offspring of the Gods is gripped by human terror and the shadow of doom. Light born of heaven, stop her, hold her back. We beg you to drive from this house the miserable, blood-stained Erinnys pursued by demons! Your pains in childbirth were wasted, wasted the bearing of those near and dear to you, woman who escaped through the Pass of Fear and sped in flight past the dark-blue Clashing Crags! Alas for her! Why has savage anger stirred the depths of her soul until only pitiless murder can repay her injuries? Vengeance falls harshly upon mortals who spill their family's blood. It cries out from the earth, a voice from the Gods, terrifying the killers upon whose homes it will descend. (The Children cry out from inside).
CHILD 1. What can I do? How can I escape from my mother's hands?
CHILD 2. I do not know, my dearest brother. Death has come for us!

CHORUS. That cry! Can you hear it, the children's cry! Miserable creature! Woman with an accursed fate! Should I go inside? My heart is shouting, "Save the children from the murder closing in on them!"
CHILD 1. Yes, by the Gods, come and help us! We desperately need you.
CHILD 2. The sword has caught us in its deadly net, and there is no escape!

CHORUS. Wretched woman! What stone is your breast made of, what steel was used to shape your heart, that you are determined to kill the babies you bore with the very hands that lovingly embraced them? I have heard of only one woman in the past who attacked her own loved ones: Ino, driven mad by the Gods when Zeus's bride chased her from her home to wander lost and alone. Standing at the edge of a sea-cliff, she fell, poor woman! Guilt for her children's blood dragged her feet down into the salt water, and she died beside both her children. What more dreadful horror can still be done? Marriage bed of women, heavy with anguish, what harm you have already brought upon humanity, how many forms of ruin! (Jason enters).

JASON. Women standing near this house, is Medea, who has done these terrible things, still inside, or has she fled? She will have to hide beneath the earth or lift herself on wings into the farthest heaven, or else face the royal family's revenge. Does she imagine she can kill the country's rulers and walk out of this house unharmed? But it is my sons I care about, not her. Those she has injured will repay her injury. I have come to save my children's lives, so that the relatives of the dead do not, to my sorrow, take revenge upon them for their mother's wicked murders.
CHORUS. Unhappy Jason, you do not know how deep into misery you have fallen, or you would never have spoken like that.
JASON. What is it now? Does she intend to kill me as well?
CHORUS. Your sons have died. Their own mother killed them.
JASON. My misery! What are you telling me? Woman, your words have killed me!
CHORUS. Think of your children as no longer living. That is the truth.
JASON. What? She killed them? Where did it happen, inside the house or outside?
CHORUS. Open the doors and you will see the bodies of your children.

JASON. Servants, pull back the bolts at once! Unbar these doors so that I can see the double horror, my dead children and their mother, and kill her in return. (Medea appears above them in a chariot drawn by dragons).

MEDEA. Why are you shaking the doors and trying to break them open, searching for your dead children and the woman who killed them? Stop trying. If you want something from me, say it. Your hands will never reach me. My father's father, the Sun, has given me this chariot to protect me from an enemy's grasp.

JASON. Abomination! Woman most hateful to the Gods, to me and to all humanity, you dared plunge a sword into the little ones you bore and leave me ruined and childless! After doing this, after daring an act so unholy, can you still look upon the earth and sun? May destruction take you! Now I see clearly what I failed to see when I brought you out of a barbarian country and household into a Greek home: a total curse, a traitor to your father and the land that raised you! The Gods have hurled the thunderbolt of your guilt against me. You murdered your own brother beside his hearth before you boarded Argo with its beautiful prow. Those were your beginnings. Then you married me and became my sons' mother, only to murder them for the sake of your marriage rights. No Greek woman would have dared such a deed. Yet I lowered myself to marry you instead of one of them, a hateful, savage bride, a tigress instead of a woman, with a fiercer nature than Scylla of the Tyrrhenian sea. But no amount of abuse could pierce you; your nature is too hardened. Get away, you criminal stained with your children's blood! I can only weep for my destiny. I shall have no happiness with my newly married bride, and never speak alive to the sons I fathered and raised. Lost, lost to me!

MEDEA. I could answer your words in a long argument if Father Zeus did not already know how I have treated you and how you have treated me. You were not going to dishonour my marriage bed and then live happily, laughing at me! Nor were your princess and Kreon, your new relation by marriage, going to banish me without suffering! So call me a tigress if you like, or Scylla haunting the Tyrrhenian coast. I have torn your heart, as you deserved.
JASON. But you are grieving too; you share in my suffering!
MEDEA. Yes. Yet sorrow is a gain to me if it stops your laughter.
JASON. My children, what a wicked mother was yours!
MEDEA. My sons, your own father's lust brought you to destruction!
JASON. It was certainly not my hand that killed them.
MEDEA. No, it was your arrogance and the new marriage bonds you forged.
JASON. What, you claim a right to kill them over a marriage!
MEDEA. Do you consider that a trivial injury for a woman?
JASON. For a sensible woman, yes. But nothing could satisfy you.
MEDEA. They are alive no longer, and that will pierce your heart!
JASON. They live, alas! They will bring vengeance down upon you.
MEDEA. The Gods understand who first set this misery in motion.
JASON. Indeed they do: they understand your loathsome nature.
MEDEA. You are the loathsome one. Your bitter tongue disgusts me.
JASON. And yours disgusts me. Yet we could easily be rid of one another.
MEDEA. How? What would I have to do? I would welcome that.
JASON. Give me my dead children so I may bury them and mourn.

MEDEA. Never. I shall bury them with my own hands, carrying them to the sanctuary of Mountain Hêrê, so that no enemy can outrage them by violating their grave. I shall require this land of Sisyphus to hold a solemn festival and rites of atonement for this unholy murder. As for me, I am going to the land of Erechtheus to live with Aigeus, Pandion's son. You, foul man, will meet the foul death you deserve: a piece of Argo's wreck will strike your skull, now that you have seen the bitter outcome of this marriage.
JASON. May the Fury who avenges children strike you, and Justice watching over murder repay you!
MEDEA. What God, what spirit would listen to your plea, you oath-breaking scoundrel who betrays a guest?
JASON. Away with you, foul creature whose own deed killed her children!
MEDEA. Go back into your house and lead your bride from there to her grave!
JASON. I go, a desolate father, robbed of both sons from my home!
MEDEA. You do not yet know true grief. Wait until your old age arrives.
JASON. My children, whom I love above everything!
MEDEA. Their mother loved them. You did not.
JASON. And yet their mother killed them!
MEDEA. So that you would be caught in the net you had spread for me.
JASON. How miserable I am! In my grief I long to press my lips against my sons' beloved lips.
MEDEA. So now you call for them, now you want to kiss them, after rejecting them before?
JASON. By the Gods, give me just this much: let me touch my children's sweet, soft bodies!
MEDEA. No. Every plea you make is wasted on the air.

JASON. Zeus, do you hear how she rejects me, what outrage I am suffering from that loathsome woman who murdered her children, that mother tigress? Yet in my helplessness and disgrace I mourn my loved ones. I call high heaven to bear witness; I ask God to hear this declaration: you have killed my sons and prevent my hands from touching them or laying their bodies in the earth! If only I had never fathered them, rather than live to see them destroyed by you today!

CHORUS. Every destiny belongs to Zeus on Olympus, and he reveals it. The Gods bring many things about that no one hoped for. What we expected, they choose not to fulfil; they open roads our eyes could never see. This astonishing event has happened so. (All leave).
